Superposition

Networks represent more features than dimensions using overlapping directions. Elhage et al., 2022 ↗

Approximation

In brief

Independent toy studies reproduce networks storing more features than dimensions through overlapping directions as features become sparser, though geometry depends on architecture and training. Independent studies also find distributed or recoverable sparse features in real models, but evidence is indirect and thin at large scales. Neurons responding to several features do not by themselves establish superposition, and capacity shortage as their general explanation is contested. Whether sparse autoencoders recover complete, stable, unique feature units is also contested. Some features require multiple dimensions; reproducibility, geometry and interpretability remain open problems.

Papers to start with: Elhage et al., 2022; Scherlis et al., 2022; Lecomte et al., 2023

Claims

SupportsLimitsChallenges
V1Toy networks superpose sparse features as near-orthogonal directions, with sparsity transitions and regular geometry 43350 Suggested status R2independently reproducedIndependent groups reproduce each part of this picture in toy models, each in its own setting: models pack more features into each dimension as sparsity rises, directions are nearly orthogonal in some settings but not under strong bottleneck pressure, and the geometry is regular (polygons, or close to an equiangular tight frame, where all pairs of directions overlap equally). None of these studies checks every part, results depend on weight decay, activation function, dropout and feature correlations, and some toy mixture-of-experts models show no clear phase change.
Original resultElhage et al., 2022 ↗

They trained small linear and ReLU toy models on sparse synthetic features with fewer hidden dimensions than features, sweeping sparsity and feature importance.

With dense features the models keep only the most important features, like PCA; as sparsity rises, ReLU models store more features than dimensions, first as antipodal pairs (two features at opposite ends of one direction), in a phase change that also depends on relative feature importance. With equal importance, features form regular shapes (triangles, tetrahedra, pentagons using 2/5 of a dimension per feature, square antiprisms), and the antipodal-pair arrangement, at 1/2 dimension per feature, stays put over a range of sparsity (a sticky plateau).

The Geometry of Superposition — Uniform Superposition

ReLU output model · Measured per-feature dimensionality and inspected feature-vector geometry · Sparsity: varied; specific values not stated; Importance: uniform

Feature dimensionality and geometric arrangement: Reported clusters at dimensionalities 3/4 (tetrahedron), 2/3 (triangle), 1/2 (antipodal pair), 2/5 (pentagon), and 3/8 (square antiprism). (baseline: 0 denotes a feature not learned; 1 denotes a dedicated dimension)

The Geometry of Superposition — Feature Dimensionality; Why These Geometric Structures?

ReLU output model · Changed the sparsity of one feature while leaving other features uniform · Uniform features: importance I = 1; activation density 1 − S = 0.05; Varied feature: one feature made more or less sparse

Feature geometry and whether the varied feature is represented: Changing sparsity deforms the pentagon; making the feature sufficiently sparse produces a phase change to two digons, with the varied feature at zero. (baseline: Uniform case gives a regular pentagon)

The Geometry of Superposition — Non-Uniform Superposition, Perturbing a Single Feature

ReLU output model · Varied sparsity of paired features that activate together · Correlation: features in each pair always activate together; their non-zero values are uncorrelated; Sparsity: varied; specific values not stated

Feature geometry and representation: In the very sparse regime, features form a hexagon with correlated features side-by-side; as sparsity decreases, pairs progressively collapse into their principal components, and the dense solution becomes equivalent to PCA.

The Geometry of Superposition — Correlated and Anticorrelated Features, Collapsing of Correlated Features

larger toy model · Visualized WᵀW for two sets of correlated features · Correlation: two sets of co-occurring correlated features

Within-set feature geometry: The authors report a local almost-orthogonal basis: correlated feature sets considered in isolation are nearly orthogonal, despite the model overall being in superposition.

The Geometry of Superposition — Correlated and Anticorrelated Features, Local Almost-Orthogonal Bases

small toy models · Compared organization of correlated and anticorrelated feature sets · Correlation: correlated sets activate together; anticorrelated sets allow only one feature in a set to be active at a time

Feature-vector arrangement under correlation structure: Correlated features are reported to prefer orthogonal directions, then proximity when orthogonality fails, and principal-component collapse when capacity is insufficient; anticorrelated features prefer interference, especially negative interference.

The Geometry of Superposition — Correlated and Anticorrelated Features

ReLU hidden layer toy model · Visualized weights and neuron feature mixtures across sparsity levels; selected the lowest-loss model · Sparsity: varied; specific values not stated; Fits per visualized model: 1000; Selection: model with lowest loss

Monosemantic versus polysemantic neurons and feature-to-neuron alignment: Monosemantic neurons occur in some sparsity regimes and polysemantic neurons in others; both can occur in the same model. Polysemantic solutions are described as structured and neuron-aligned.

Superposition in a Privileged Basis — Visualizing Superposition in Terms of Neurons

absolute-value ReLU hidden layer toy model · Trained the model to compute absolute value while varying feature sparsity · Task: y = abs(x); Sparsity: varied; specific values not stated

Feature mixtures in neurons while computing the target: At sufficient sparsity, the model uses superposition to represent more features than neurons and still usefully approximates the computation. In intermediate regimes, some neurons are pure while a subset are highly polysemantic; neurons representing the most important features tend to be monosemantic. (baseline: In the dense regime, each neuron represents a single feature)

Computation in Superposition — Superposition vs Sparsity

absolute-value ReLU hidden layer toy model · Compared the learned computation with the non-superposed absolute-value construction · Task: y = abs(x)

Hidden-neuron representation used for the computation: The model computes absolute value with a positive-side and a negative-side neuron for each input feature, as expected without superposition. (baseline: Without superposition, two hidden neurons are needed per feature)

Regular-polygon feature layouts were proven critical points of the loss and held most Bayesian posterior mass. Zhong-Tian Chen et al., 2023 ↗

Dynamical versus Bayesian Phase Transitions in a Toy Model of Superposition

High-sparsity-limit TMS, r=2, c=4,5,6; Bayesian posterior at n>400 (c=6) and the ranges shown for c=4,5

Regular k-gons with k>r were proven to be critical points, and posterior mass concentrated on k-gon phases. This was a 4-gon for c=4, a shift from 4-gon to 5-gon for c=5, and a shift from 5-gon to 6-gon at 600≤n≤700 for c=6.

A residual ReLU network stored tokens as overlapping sparse hashes in fewer dimensions. Alex Gibson, 2026 ↗

Neural Networks learn Bloom Filters

Trained 1-layer residual ReLU network, vocabulary much larger than residual width.

Tokens were stored as overlapping sparse hashes in fewer dimensions than the vocabulary size, and the overlap caused interference in the form of rare false positives.

Single trained toy attention heads (dhead 8 or 16), dense continuous Gaussian latents, r1 + r2 > dhead

Losses raising error to powers above 2 gave features overlapping sparse neuron sets, spreading error evenly. Francisco Ferreira da Silva et al., 2026 ↗

Compressed Computation under $L^4$ Loss is likely Computation in Superposition

Loss exponent >2 (L2.5–L8), p=0.02, 100 features/50 neurons, axis-aligned and embedded; also the 1000/500 scale-up

Per-feature error was spread evenly (CV 0.028–0.046, 0.031 embedded, 0.06 at 1000/500), and each feature had a sparse codeword of 5–7 neurons in a near-biregular code with small overlaps. Swap tests decoded correctly in 100% of cases, and the decoder was close to the pseudoinverse (0.996).

Quadratic toy model, analytic and numerical, across quadratic, ReLU and GeLU activations

quadratic model · Analytically derives and numerically illustrates optimal feature-capacity allocation as feature importance and kurtosis vary. · Importance: one feature's relative importance varies against the others; Sparsity: varied through input kurtosis; Features/dimensions: 6 features in 3 neurons for Figure 4

Optimal capacity allocated to each feature: For k > 3, sufficiently unimportant features are ignored, sufficiently important features are fully represented, and an intermediate range receives fractional capacity; for k ≤ 3, features are either ignored or fully represented. The intermediate, partially represented region occurs at higher sparsity.

our toy model · Compares numerical capacity-allocation phase diagrams across activation functions. · Activation: quadratic, ReLU, and GeLU; Features/dimensions: 6 in 3 displayed; the text says 6 in 5 is similar; Sparsity: varied

Sections 3.7 and Figure 7

efficient embedding matrices · Characterizes the geometry of matrices that saturate the total-capacity bound. · Capacity: efficient matrices with total capacity equal to D

Embedding-vector geometry and interference: The paper proves that efficient matrices have a block-semiorthogonal form. Features interfere within a block but not across blocks; a feature reaching capacity 1 becomes orthogonal and separates into a new block.

Related findings4 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Networks can compute nonlinear functions in superposition 20 studies

Sparse superposed codes can support nonlinear computation. How accurate, how large and how deep that computation can be is limited by interference, readout, activation function, training objective and how labels are built.

  • Splitting neurons by Boolean clause gives 99.4% accuracy; dense networks with equal nonzero-weight counts get 78.7%. Linghao Kong et al., 2025 ↗
  • Theory gives dimension thresholds ~k log m for pairwise conjunctions (k active of m random-dictionary features). Xiao-Yu Li et al., 2026 ↗
  • A hand-coded ReLU MLP holds 557 switchable vector-rotation circuits, but errors grow superlinearly with depth. Linda Linsefors, 2025 ↗
Features emerge and reorganize during training 18 studies

Feature emergence, rotation, consolidation and geometry change over training. Inferred transitions and the strength of superposition depend on the objective, input statistics and measurement method.

  • Toy-model Bayesian posterior shifts from pentagonal to hexagonal feature arrangements at 600–700 samples, as theory predicts. Zhong-Tian Chen et al., 2023 ↗
  • A forced random superposition bottleneck gives power-law loss-decay exponents near 1 mid-training, as learnable embeddings do. Z. Chen et al., 2026 ↗
Superposition geometry predicts adversarial vulnerability 9 studies

The interference geometry of superposed features can predict adversarial vulnerability and transfer. How robustness training changes this depends on geometry, task, capacity, layer and attack type.

  • In toy models, adversarial vulnerability correlates with features per dimension (r≈0.99) under Elhage et al.-style attacks. Liv Gorton et al., 2025 ↗
  • Toy-model robust accuracy falls as k/m (features per bottleneck dimension) rises, reaching 18.7% at m=2. Xijia Che, 2026 ↗
Toy models store data points in superposition 2 studies

Toy bottleneck networks can store individual training examples in superposition, and can shift from memorizing examples to learning features. Whether and how double descent shows up depends on training conditions.

  • Weight decay removes the double-descent test-loss bump between memorizing and learning features; more epochs enlarge it. Superposition, Memorization, and Doub… ↗
V4Real models spread features across many neurons, or hold sparse features SAEs can recover 125872 Suggested status R2independently reproducedMany independent groups report features spread across neurons or recovered by sparse autoencoders (SAEs), in protein, vision and audio models and in language models such as Pythia-70M and Gemma-2-9B, with thinner evidence above 10B parameters, such as Gemma-3-27B, and none for models known to exceed 100B. The evidence is indirect and depends on layer, dictionary and metric: randomized models can match trained ones on automated interpretation, and the two studies that challenge the claim find problems only with particular dictionaries.

Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models

Pythia-70M residual stream (especially early layers) and Pythia-410M layer-11 IOI patching

SAE features scored higher than neuron-basis, random, PCA and ICA directions on autointerpretability, including under random-only scoring. In Pythia-410M they localized IOI with fewer, smaller patches than PCA or a non-sparse dictionary.

Finding Neurons in a Haystack

Early MLP layers (1–3) of Pythia 1B, compound-word (n-gram) features

Summing a small number of polysemantic neurons recovered compound-word features with near-perfect separation. The neuron basis also beat random bases, which favours superposition over a rotated basis.

Related findings6 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Concepts spread across many units, directions and layers 38 studies

A concept or behavior can depend on many neurons, directions, feature groups or layers that share, duplicate or compensate for each other's roles. These contributions shift under compression, pruning and scale.

  • Six coarse concepts stay linearly decodable in a width-128 distilled model, close to its teacher. Nilesh Sarkar et al., 2026 ↗
  • Optimized cones of directions flip truth answers; success varies by model and cone dimension. Stanley Yu et al., 2025 ↗
Individual neurons range from narrow to mixed selectivity 35 studies

Native neurons and adapter directions can be narrowly tuned, mixed or spread across variables. Measured selectivity depends on architecture, depth, context and method, and on its own does not show that limited capacity causes mixing.

  • 31% of inspected ResNet-18 neurons fire for unrelated concepts; 69% learn compositional abstractions. Jesse Mu et al., 2020 ↗
  • Autointerp judges 62% of SAE latents on LoRA states monosemantic, versus 22% of LoRA directions. Jake Ward et al., 2025 ↗
  • Gemma-2-2B neurons selected by gradient-weighted activation change fire more densely than average neurons, with sharper peaks. Giuseppe Birardi, 2026 ↗
Representations keep dense, anisotropic and basis-aligned structure 19 studies

Distributed representations can keep dense, anisotropic, low-rank or coordinate-aligned structure. Effective dimension and basis preferences depend on architecture, site, depth and method.

  • Usually, attention outputs have effective rank about 60% of width; MLP and residual streams about 90%. Junxuan Wang et al., 2025 ↗
  • Sampled Qwen3-32B layer-0 neurons are heavy-tailed, and kurtosis tracks lexical concentration (ρ=0.55). Si-Da Liu et al., 2026 ↗
  • Toy-model hidden dimensions have more interdependent signs (mutual information) than the authors report for real transformers. V. Nalagatla et al., 2026 ↗
Feature pathways reveal reuse and separate meanings 15 studies

Tracing features through upstream pathways can separate the meanings of a polysemantic unit and expose compositional reuse. Circuit connectivity and decompositions depend on training, basis and analysis.

  • In two ViT-B neurons, unrelated concepts share 18% of upstream pathways, related ones 42%. Sehyun Lee et al., 2026 ↗
  • A training-time decorrelation penalty cuts the downstream components reading each concept from about 21 to 1.4. M. Oskin, 2026 ↗
  • Pythia 2.8B still recalls athletes' sports with later attention mean-ablated; an MLP-only version reaches 94% accuracy. Senthooran Rajamanoharan, 2023 ↗
Networks damp or amplify perturbations depending on direction 8 studies

Networks suppress or amplify perturbations unevenly across directions and can favor candidate feature directions over mixtures of them. Apparent error correction depends on direction, layer, dictionary and baseline.

  • In a two-layer denoising network, perturbation-response exponents are higher along true feature directions than feature mixtures. Francisco Ferreira da Silva et al., 2026 ↗
  • Parent SAE features amplify slightly more than children, but SAE features are not local maxima. Dmitry Vaintrob, 2026 ↗
Population directions predict brain responses better than units 3 studies

Directions across a population can be more interpretable, or better predictors of biological visual responses, than individual artificial or biological units.

  • Sparse-autoencoder latents predict fMRI in the human ventral visual stream better than ResNet50 and ViT neurons. André Longon et al., 2025 ↗

How it works

V2Are neurons polysemantic because features compete for limited capacity? 19141 Suggested status CcontestedIndependent toy-model studies confirm that, with the right sparsity and importance, important features get their own dimensions while the rest share dimensions. Capacity shortage as the general explanation is contested: polysemanticity also appears in networks with more neurons than features, and language-model evidence is mostly indirect, as in a Gemma distillation study where which features are kept depends on capacity but there is limited evidence that features share dimensions.
Original resultElhage et al., 2022 ↗

They trained small ReLU toy models, varying feature sparsity and the relative importance of an extra feature from 0.1 to 10.

Whether a feature was ignored, given its own dimension or shared in superposition changed in phase transitions with sparsity and importance, and superposition needed sparsity. In a model computing absolute value, intermediate sparsity left some neurons pure and others highly polysemantic, and the neurons for the most important features tended to be monosemantic.

Measurements and conditions (5)

Toy Models of Superposition

ReLU output model · Swept the extra feature's importance and feature sparsity; compared not learned, superposed, and orthogonally represented outcomes · Extra feature importance: 0.1 to 10; Sparsity: 1.0 to 0.01; Fits per point: 10; highest-loss model discarded

Optimal encoding of the extra feature: The paper reports an empirical and theoretical phase change: sparsity is necessary for superposition, and the encoding strategy also varies with relative feature importance. (baseline: Compared configurations include ignoring the extra feature, dedicating the dimension to it, or encoding both features antipodally)

Superposition as a Phase Change

ReLU output model · Changed the sparsity of one feature while leaving other features uniform · Uniform features: importance I = 1; activation density 1 − S = 0.05; Varied feature: one feature made more or less sparse

The Geometry of Superposition — Non-Uniform Superposition, Perturbing a Single Feature

ReLU hidden layer toy model · Visualized weights and neuron feature mixtures across sparsity levels; selected the lowest-loss model · Sparsity: varied; specific values not stated; Fits per visualized model: 1000; Selection: model with lowest loss

Monosemantic versus polysemantic neurons and feature-to-neuron alignment: Monosemantic neurons occur in some sparsity regimes and polysemantic neurons in others; both can occur in the same model. Polysemantic solutions are described as structured and neuron-aligned.

Superposition in a Privileged Basis — Visualizing Superposition in Terms of Neurons

absolute-value ReLU hidden layer toy model · Trained the model to compute absolute value while varying feature sparsity · Task: y = abs(x); Sparsity: varied; specific values not stated

Feature mixtures in neurons while computing the target: At sufficient sparsity, the model uses superposition to represent more features than neurons and still usefully approximates the computation. In intermediate regimes, some neurons are pure while a subset are highly polysemantic; neurons representing the most important features tend to be monosemantic. (baseline: In the dense regime, each neuron represents a single feature)

Polysemanticity and Capacity in Neural Networks

Quadratic toy model; Anthropic model in the 6-in-5 setting

In the quadratic toy model, important features received full capacity, unimportant features were ignored, and an intermediate range shared capacity. In the 6-in-5 setting, a much more important feature was not left superposed.

Cited measurements (3)

quadratic model · Analytically derives and numerically illustrates optimal feature-capacity allocation as feature importance and kurtosis vary. · Importance: one feature's relative importance varies against the others; Sparsity: varied through input kurtosis; Features/dimensions: 6 features in 3 neurons for Figure 4

Optimal capacity allocated to each feature: For k > 3, sufficiently unimportant features are ignored, sufficiently important features are fully represented, and an intermediate range receives fractional capacity; for k ≤ 3, features are either ignored or fully represented. The intermediate, partially represented region occurs at higher sparsity.

Sections 3.2 and 3.4

Related findings4 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Attention heads and weights can multiplex several functions 12 studies

Attention heads and weight components can carry several functions at once or spread one function across many components. Intervention effects depend on capacity and inputs, and these findings alone do not show superposition in activations.

  • In Gemma-2b, individually helpful head knockouts don't add: the top 3 together beat the top 10. Gao-Tang Li et al., 2025 ↗
  • In a four-head toy model learning five skip trigrams (A…B→C), one was spread across all heads. cmathw, 2024 ↗
  • Ablating head L1H6 turns off 443 of 450 induction features and hurts other code features. Connor Kissane, 2024 ↗
Feature frequency and training conditions shape dictionary allocation 12 studies

Prevalence, co-occurrence, variance, scale and learning conditions affect how strongly features are represented and how dictionaries allocate latents. There is no universal rule that frequent features get dedicated units.

  • 76% of a layer-8 residual-stream SAE's features fire on single-token inputs; authors blame imbalanced training n-grams. tdooms, 2024 ↗
Overlapping codes accompany retrieval failures and forgetting 10 studies

Overlapping codes and competing contextual states can come with worse retrieval, composition and retention. The size of the effect depends on training coverage, state weighting, feature strength and update conditions.

  • Reweighting superposed reasoning states lowers a trained router's success and raises false alarms on inactive keys. Hong-Yuan Gu et al., 2026 ↗
  • Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-1.5B on facts causes far more forgetting when keys are meaningful rather than random UUIDs. Guy Kaplan et al., 2026 ↗
Code geometry sets capacity and loss scaling 6 studies

How much a representation can store, and how loss scales, depend on code geometry, learned embeddings, how many features are active at once, and the superposition regime.

  • Learned embeddings merge inputs that share an output, cutting the dimension needed for error-free recall. Vivien Cabannes et al., 2023 ↗
V5Are sparse autoencoder features complete, stable, canonical units of the model's representation? 4815775 Suggested status CcontestedThis is contested: toy settings where the dictionary's width and sparsity match the true features, and frequent, simple features in small models, often give stable, recoverable features, but many studies find features that split or absorb each other as dictionary size changes, shift across seeds and training data, and miss information the model uses. Evidence at 10–100B parameters is thin and does not test seed stability or canonicality (whether there is one unique set of feature units).

The rating for models of 10 to 100 billion parameters changed from contested to undetermined: after checking, results at that size show only partial shortfalls, one study that reports a clear failure pools a 27-billion-parameter model with smaller ones without giving a separate value for it, and none tests whether features stay the same across training runs or are canonical. The overall rating stays contested, based on results in toy and smaller models.

Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output model activations · Scanned learning rate and ℓ1 coefficient and selected the lowest-loss and highest-monosemanticity realizations from five runs. · Amplitude correlation C: 1; Learning rate: 3×10−5, 10−4, 3×10−4, 10−3, 3×10−3; ℓ1 coefficient λ: 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1; Realizations per setting: 5

Monosemanticity of learned SAE features: Only λ=0.01 with learning rate 3×10−4 achieved a mostly monosemantic realization; it was not perfectly monosemantic. (baseline: Underlying features in the synthetic data)

Results — Correlated Feature Amplitudes

Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output model activations · Trained SAEs on data with uncorrelated feature amplitudes and assessed whether they learned composed pairs. · Amplitude correlation C: 0; Data: two-hot vectors with independently sampled feature magnitudes; Learning rate and λ: parameters studied in the preceding sweep

Recovery of composed pairs rather than underlying features: SAEs almost uniformly learned perfect composed pairs across the parameters studied. (baseline: Underlying features in the synthetic data)

Results — Uncorrelated Feature Amplitudes

Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output model activations · Examined realizations at high learning rate and low ℓ1 coefficient in the uncorrelated-amplitude sweep. · Amplitude correlation C: 0; Learning rate and λ: high learning rate and low λ

Monosemanticity versus composed-feature solutions: Some realizations found monosemantic features, but other realizations had lower loss and learned polysemantic composed pairs. (baseline: Underlying features in the synthetic data)

Results — Uncorrelated Feature Amplitudes

Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output model activations · Added a regularization term based on the mean of the lower-triangular decoder cosine-similarity matrix, without absolute values. · Cosine penalty: coefficient × mean(tril(S))

Ability to find monosemantic features: The added term did not improve monosemantic feature recovery; the models found the same solution as above. (baseline: SAE without the added cosine-similarity term)

Results — Does a Cosine Similarity Loss Term Fix This Problem?

Sparse autoencoders trained on the ReLU output model activations · Added a regularization term based on the mean absolute value of the lower-triangular decoder cosine-similarity matrix. · Cosine penalty: coefficient × mean(abs(tril(S)))

Ability to find monosemantic features: The models found either the same solution or one where some feature decoder vectors collapsed; the term did not improve monosemantic feature recovery. (baseline: SAE without the added cosine-similarity term)

Results — Does a Cosine Similarity Loss Term Fix This Problem?

Mixed data with p(one-hot)=0.75, where the true features are identifiable

On mixed data where the true features are identifiable, more of the lowest-loss SAEs recovered them, but not robustly across learning rate and λ.

Theory shows optimal SAEs shrink or zero out polysemantic features at ordinary sparsity. Jing-Yi Cui et al., 2025 ↗

On the Limits of Sparse Autoencoders: A Theoretical Framework and Reweighted Remedy

General (non-extreme) sparsity in the paper's linear superposition model and synthetic toy setup

The closed-form optimum shrank or zeroed polysemantic features, for example (1.0, 0.8) → (0.2, 0) and (0.7, 0.5, 0.3) → (0.3, 0, 0), and in synthetic data latents mixed several ground-truth features at lower sparsity.

theoretical SAE framework · Derives an optimal SAE solution and analyzes its ground-truth feature recovery · Geometry: columns of Wp form digons/polygons; Sparsity: general conditions

Ground-truth feature recovery from SAE latents: The optimum is Wp transpose (up to row reordering and zero padding); recovered features can shrink or vanish and generally do not recover the ground truth.

Toy Models of Feature Absorption in SAEs

Untied toy SAEs with perfectly co-occurring features (with and without superposition), or imperfect co-occurrence at a high L1 penalty

SAE with 4 latents (SAELens) · Train an SAE on synthetic features with feature 1 firing only when feature 0 also fires. · Cooccurrence: feature 1 only fires with feature 0; feature 1 overall firing rate remains 5%; Other features: features 2 and 3 remain independent; L1 coefficient: 3e-5

Feature recovery and latent firing pattern: Latent 0 has a hole when feature 1 is active; latent 3, which tracks feature 1, absorbs the feature 0 direction. Features 2 and 3 are reported as unaffected and recovered perfectly. The post states that only one SAE latent fires when features 0 and 1 are both active. Feature co-occurrence causes absorption

SAE with 4 latents (SAELens) · Train the SAE with feature 0's firing magnitude varying while feature 1 co-occurs with it. · Cooccurrence: feature 1 fires only with feature 0; Feature 0 magnitude: standard deviation 0.1

Feature recovery and latent firing pattern: The feature 0 latent still has a hole and the feature 1 decoder has absorbed feature 0, but absorption is weaker. When both features have magnitude 1.0, the feature 0 latent fires weakly; when feature 0's magnitude drops to 0.75, it turns off. (baseline: True feature representations and firing patterns)

Magnitude variance causes partial absorption

SAE with 4 latents (SAELens) · Train a new SAE with a higher another measurement coefficient under imperfect co-occurrence. · Cooccurrence: feature 1 co-occurs with feature 0 95% of the time and fires on its own 5% of the time; L1 coefficient: increased from 5e-3 to 2e-2

Appendix D; Figure 12

Related findings5 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

SAE features stay partly polysemantic and context-dependent 43 studies

Dictionary latents and their labels need not match one stable human concept. How well a description predicts activations or effects varies with the examples, activation range, context and validation used.

  • Most sampled GemmaScope features had different input and output meanings (70.7% of 215). De-Wen Liu et al., 2026 ↗
  • Automated label misses a Gemma2-2B latent's secondary trigger, present in about 40% of top inputs. T. White, 2024 ↗
  • Auto-interp descriptions predict ablation effects at ρ=0.69–0.81 on PRDB but only 0.36–0.62 on COLING. Liam Dugan et al., 2026 ↗
Feature identities depend on how they are measured 30 studies

Feature identity, polysemanticity and causal attribution depend on coordinates, decoder class, constraints, seeds, thresholds and controls. Stable statistics or subspaces need not mean the individual units are canonical.

  • ReLU decoding of 1-D antipodal codes nears R²=1 as sparsity grows; linear caps at 1/2. Dai Shi et al., 2026 ↗
  • In synthetic data, features sharing a rank-2 subspace seldom reappear across seeds, but the subspace does. Gleb Gerasimov et al., 2026 ↗
  • Steering projections correlate with log-mass contrast; reversing label–mass alignment nearly reverses the direction. Man-Jiang Yu et al., 2026 ↗
Sparsity objectives favor absorbed and mixed latents 20 studies

Feature co-occurrence, hierarchy and sparsity objectives can favor absorbed or mixed latents even when the model is not short of capacity. Trained dictionaries, and fixes proposed for these problems, may not reach the best exact sparse code.

  • A closed-form L0 boundary for favoring parent over child features matches 30/30 synthetic, 12/16 trained-SAE settings. Jin-Yuan Zhang et al., 2026 ↗
  • A feature-mixing (hedging) SAE beats a truncated true-feature SAE on MSE at k=4 (0.42 vs 0.53). chanind, 2025 ↗
SAE codes shift with context and small perturbations 12 studies

Which SAE features fire, and what they represent locally, can change with context, paraphrase, time and perturbations. Stability depends on thresholds, position, depth, training objective and model.

  • Only 11.7% of SAE features for bare concept names survive in contextual prompts. M. Wenzel, 2026 ↗
  • GCG attacks perturbing one token cut top-k SAE feature overlap with the original to about 20–30%. Aaron J. Li et al., 2025 ↗
  • Noun latents silenced by added adjectives often fire upstream; most are near threshold, except in Mistral. Nikolai Bolik et al., 2026 ↗
Graph-level descriptions can work without canonical atoms 12 studies

Encoder and decoder proxies can misdescribe what a feature does mechanistically. Graph structure and downstream metrics can still give predictive descriptions without relying on canonical individual SAE atoms.

  • SAE-encoding every Gemma 2 steering vector, even a zero vector, gives the same top two features. Harry Mayne et al., 2024 ↗
  • Attribution-graph structure predicts probe accuracy (Gemma ρ=0.91), but in Llama only weakly within a concept. V. Palit et al., 2026 ↗
V6Are superposed features one-dimensional directions rather than multi-dimensional structures? 9186 Suggested status CcontestedSeveral independent groups find features that do not reduce to single directions, such as cyclic day and month representations in Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B and ring-shaped structure in Gemma 2. Single directions still work for some features, such as sentiment, so the claim that superposed features are always one-dimensional is contested.
Original resultElhage et al., 2022 ↗

The original paper did not test this claim.

Representative studies

  • SupportsExtra subspace dimensions added nothing over a single sentiment direction in Pythia and GPT-2. O. Hollinsworth et al., 2024 ↗
  • LimitsMost bilinear-autoencoder features on Qwen3.5-0.8B spanned very few dimensions, but a tail spanned more. Thomas Dooms et al., 2026 ↗
  • ChallengesDays, months and years formed irreducible 2-D circular features in GPT-2 small and Mistral 7B. circular multi-dimensional features ↗

Related findings5 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Linear readouts expose concepts, with limits 35 studies

Linear probes and vector differences expose semantic, factual and task information. Which axes are recovered and which shifts work depend on the model, layer, interface, context and controls.

  • In LLaMA-2-7B, word-pair differences align with a shared concept direction for 26 of 27 concepts. Kiho Park et al., 2023 ↗
  • A Qwen3-4B probe predicts code correctness at AUC 0.881; a prompt-length baseline reaches 0.657. C. Di Cicco, 2026 ↗
  • A weights-derived probe recovers Pythia 2.8B athlete-sport lookups at 98%, versus the model's 100%. Senthooran Rajamanoharan, 2023 ↗
Features form semantic neighborhoods, families and hierarchies 34 studies

Populations of dictionary features can form semantic neighborhoods, hierarchies and conditional or temporal families. How coherent they are depends on the model, selection and regularization, and statistical opposition is not the same as semantic opposition.

  • Selected neighboring SAE features form a semantic cluster with higher cosines than a random control. Zheng-Fu He et al., 2024 ↗
  • Curated Qwen-VL-Chat SAE features on CLEVR form semantic-category blocks above random coherence. Yun-Xiang Zhou, 2026 ↗
  • Graph-learning AG-SAE assigns 23.55% of Gemma-2-2B child features multiple parents, with better-validated links than vanilla SAEs. Xiao-Zuo Shen et al., 2026 ↗
Concepts can live in multidimensional subspaces and manifolds 33 studies

Concepts and task variables can occupy multidimensional subspaces, manifolds or structured feature families rather than single directions. Distinct variables can also share directions when read out by magnitude or nonlinearly.

  • Single linear-regression (TDR) axes predict motion and colour in context-dependent Mante-task RNNs; ablation barely changes accuracy. Shreya Saha et al., 2026 ↗
  • On additive manifold mixtures, block-sparse featurizers recover blocks far better than TopK SAEs. Thomas Fel et al., 2026 ↗
  • Gradient-reversal training against country drops linear-probe AUC to near-chance 0.519; an MLP probe still reaches 0.974. IgorPereverzevDev, 2026 ↗
Geometry encodes values, but measures need task-specific checks 16 studies

Concept geometry can encode hierarchies and continuous values. Similarity, orthogonality and dimension need task-specific metrics and controls before they can predict recovery, causal equivalence or independence.

  • Steering along a learned time manifold shifts year completions, working best around layers 8–14. Alexander Modell, 2026 ↗
  • A LoRA-learned direction and a mean-difference direction are nearly orthogonal, yet their downstream effects partly align. Anna Soligo et al., 2025 ↗
  • In synthetic settings, signal-to-noise ratio and alignment predict target-direction recovery; intrinsic dimension does not. Prajjwal Bhattarai et al., 2026 ↗
Attention computation runs through sparse, low-rank channels 11 studies

Attention computation and communication between modules can be broken into sparse or low-rank parts. The relevant dimension depends on feature type, normalization and downstream readout.

  • Llama 3.1-8B heads filter categories with rank-1 query-key subspaces; binding by word identity needs rank 9–10. Andrew Lee et al., 2026 ↗
  • Attention-pattern transcoders for GPT2-small permit only 25,000–51,000 of about 69 million possible query-key feature pairs. keith_wynroe, 2024 ↗

V3Polysemanticity can arise without capacity pressure, so alone it is not evidence of superposition 1020 Suggested status R2independently reproducedSeveral groups independent of the original study find mixed-selective neurons, which respond to several features, in toy networks with more than enough units; the routes differ, such as the range of values the underlying source variables take, or nonlinear feature contamination, where neurons pick up extra features. One study of real transformers finds word-level (lexical) confounds in polysemanticity measurements, but it does not show polysemanticity arising without capacity pressure.

Challenges0 sources

No sources in this group.

Related findings2 groups of studies

Results that bear on this claim without testing it as worded.

Architecture and training choices shape neuron specialization 35 studies

Architecture, training method, objective, regularization, routing and pruning change a network's representation basis and how much its units specialize or share. This can happen even when the network is not short of units, and the effect on capabilities varies.

  • With L1/L2 penalties, a two-task network gives each neuron one task or leaves it unused. Jinyeop Song et al., 2024 ↗
  • Training models with k-winners-take-all self-ablation gives sparser SAE codes, more loss recovered, but higher weight L1. J. Ferrao et al., 2025 ↗
  • MoWE (MoE with disjoint expert outputs) has more specific FFN coordinates than dense or MoE models. Tavish Mankash et al., 2026 ↗
MoE experts mix specialized and shared functions 6 studies

Mixture-of-experts experts and routes can combine specialized and shared functions. How semantically broad an expert is depends on routing sparsity, layer, granularity and interacting features.

  • In gpt-oss-20b and OLMoE, each expert's top SAE latents span fewer semantic clusters than random sets. I. Lasy et al., 2026 ↗

Monitoring and steering with features

These findings are for anyone using features to detect, probe or steer behaviour: when such uses work, and what can go wrong.

Selected dictionary features can causally steer outputs 41 studies

Selected SAE or crosscoder features can causally change generation, retrieval and policy outputs. The effects depend on which features are chosen, the model, the site, the strength and timing of the intervention, and gating.

  • Zeroing one SAE latent reorders retrieval; in one example, the top result falls to 9th. Wonseok Shin et al., 2026 ↗
  • Ablating top-10 culture-selective features cuts cultural MCQ accuracy to 0.31; random ablation does not. Chenye Zou et al., 2026 ↗
  • Editing one feature in an SAE-tokenized recommender raises its exposure by 1.365 pp over controls. Ziluowen Luo et al., 2026 ↗
Decodable features are not necessarily good control handles 34 studies

That a feature is decodable, active, selective or recurring does not make it a necessary or sufficient control handle. Causal effects depend on downstream readers, selection and context, and interventions can push activations off-distribution or cause broad damage.

  • Negative-multiplier SAE steering in SD v1.5 and SDXL Turbo yields 43–61% artifact rates. E. Cassano et al., 2026 ↗
  • Among SAE features that track person names, the most selective have the smallest causal effects (r=−0.56). C. Munigety, 2026 ↗
  • Gradient-based estimates predict the sign of single-latent ablation effects in 91–97% of cases; probes in 17–35%. Yi-Feng Guo et al., 2026 ↗
Sparse codes help downstream tasks only in some settings 27 studies

Sparse codes and feature selection can improve downstream readouts, correction or adjustment. The gains depend on task, layer, budget and baseline, and do not show a general advantage.

  • SAE profiles beat dense embeddings for RNA-type kNN at layers 5 and 11, not 0. M. Hossain et al., 2026 ↗
  • An adapter on driving-planner SAE latents cuts displacement error slightly more than dense or random-encoder inputs. Manav Gagvani et al., 2026 ↗
Steering effects depend on strength, context and combination 23 studies

The effect of a feature intervention depends on its coefficient and sign, the context, how features are combined, and how the intervention is designed. It can also change behavior broadly, beyond the target.

  • Unscaled averages of coding steering vectors mostly yield refusals or jailbreaks; √n-scaling reportedly restores code output. Jacob G-W, 2024 ↗
Feature interventions change outputs beyond text models 18 studies

Interventions on dictionary features can change outputs in biological, vision, recommendation and control models. Selectivity, side effects and effectiveness vary by architecture, stream, layer and concept.

  • In the GTRS driving planner, zeroing three SAE latents raises overall score but lowers route progress. Franz Motzkus et al., 2026 ↗
  • In implicit neural representations, ablating one SAE atom hurts SIREN reconstructions locally, Fourier-feature MLP ones image-wide. Vasiliki Sideri-Lampretsa et al., 2026 ↗
Sparse features expose task and reward signals 15 studies

Sparse features can expose task-relevant, demographic or reward-related signals and support targeted interventions or training constraints. Their selectivity depends on context and model.

  • Zero-ablating GPT-4-flagged features lowers reward in two Pythia models but not GPT-Neo-125m. Luke Marks et al., 2023 ↗
Overlapping features and interventions do not add simply 13 studies

Overlap between features can predict spillover from interventions, but behavioral effects need not combine independently or additively. Reducing global correlation between dictionary atoms need not reduce the interference that actually occurs.

  • Low-interference training cuts overlap between dictionary atoms 19.2%, but overlap weighted by their activations only 0.9%. Xiao-Yang Li et al., 2026 ↗
  • Modeling pairwise interactions between steering directions predicts their combined MMLU-Pro effects better than summing individual effects. Hao-Tian Ma et al., 2026 ↗
Refusal follows one direction; harmfulness has more structure 5 studies

Refusal can be strongly driven by one dominant linear direction, while harmfulness and behavior categories keep additional, overlapping structure that depends on the method.

  • Harmfulness subcategory directions have effective rank 1, yet probes retrained after directional ablation stay accurate. Mcnair Shah et al., 2025 ↗

Training and evaluating dictionaries

These findings are for anyone building sparse dictionaries or alternatives to them: how design, training and evaluation choices change the features you get and how far to trust them.

Dictionary design choices set feature granularity 57 studies

Dictionary architecture, width, sparsity, objective and preprocessing change which features are recovered, how fine-grained they are and how useful they are. No single setting does best on every criterion.

  • On MNIST, narrow high-L0 SAEs learn digit fragments; wide low-L0 SAEs learn whole-digit features. K. Ayonrinde et al., 2024 ↗
  • On Gemma-2-2B, Matryoshka SAEs show far less feature absorption than TopK (0.056 vs 0.275). Jakub Stepien et al., 2026 ↗
  • Reconstruction-only SAE codes fail to separate author-level targets from background in Qwen. Itai Zehavi et al., 2026 ↗
Good reconstruction does not show meaningful features 49 studies

Reconstruction, sparsity, coverage, stability and interpretability scores measure different things. None of them alone shows that a dictionary has recovered meaningful features, uses its capacity, or preserves task information.

  • Untrained random dictionaries cover a CUB concept-bottleneck model's concepts better than trained SAEs (0.65 vs 0.25). Alexandre Rocchi-Henry et al., 2025 ↗
  • SAEs reconstruct random-weight BiomedParse embeddings as well as learned ones; downstream AUC stays low. Philipp Wesp et al., 2026 ↗
  • A DiT SAE explains 0.9997 of variance while using only 1.5% of its dictionary. Xinyue Xu et al., 2026 ↗
Effective dictionary size can fall far below nominal width 30 studies

SAE objectives, parameterization, preprocessing and data change dictionary coherence, feature identities, stability and how many latents are used. The usable set of features can differ greatly from the nominal width.

  • Top-k SAEs on sentence embeddings use most latents (few are dead), with little decoder-direction overlap. Wonseok Shin et al., 2026 ↗
  • A 2048-latent SAE on pathology embeddings uses only 74 latents across 7.7M patches. Su-Su Sun et al., 2025 ↗
  • GPT2-small attention-pattern transcoders keep only 144–524 of 2400 features alive. keith_wynroe, 2024 ↗
Encoder and inference choices change feature recovery 22 studies

How well sparse features are recovered depends on encoder expressivity, inference procedure, optimization, geometry and benchmark design. Reconstruction quality alone does not certify recovery.

  • On GPT-2, dictionaries with MLP encoders score higher autointerpretability than SAE or LCA dictionaries. Charles O'Neill et al., 2024 ↗
  • LISTA-Matryoshka beats the best prior SAE on the synthetic SynthSAEBench-16k; LLM transfer is unverified. chanind, 2026 ↗
Small feature sets can stand in for dense representations 19 studies

Small sets of dictionary features can preserve local neighborhoods, selected task information or the effect of a behavioral direction. How many features are needed, how faithful the substitute is, and whether it transfers depend on inputs, task, dictionary and the sparsity imposed.

  • An adaptive mask keeping about 40 SAE concepts matches dense CLIP reconstructions in test-time training. Jonas Hübotter et al., 2025 ↗
  • In Phi-3 Mini, 2–4 SAE features rebuild an effective refusal direction; sycophancy is harder. neverix, 2024 ↗
Reconstruction and replacement can lose task information 19 studies

Reconstructing activations, or replacing model parts with sparse ones, can lose task information. Fidelity varies with layer, domain, repeated encoding and the replacement architecture.

  • Layer-24 SAEs reconstruct other layers poorly; Gemma's fraction of unexplained variance reaches 24.05 at layer 41. V. Menon et al., 2026 ↗
Supervised and compositional objectives reshape dictionary features 12 studies

Supervised, task-aware and compositional training objectives can change which latents represent each concept and can improve some semantic or recovery measures. They do not establish canonical atomic features.

  • Meta-SAEs trained on decoder directions explain 42% of Matryoshka SAE decoder variance but 55% for BatchTopK. Bart Bussmann et al., 2025 ↗
  • An SAE trained for predicting CLIP's errors yields more directions humans judge to match one class. Jie-Shu Ma et al., 2026 ↗
Supervised subspaces can beat neurons and SAE units 12 studies

Supervised subspaces and alternative decompositions can isolate task variables better than single neurons or unsupervised SAE units in some settings.

  • On Llama-3.1, supervised subspaces found by DAS beat SAE featurizers on RAVEL entity-attribute and multiple-choice tasks. Dana Arad et al., 2025 ↗
  • A training-free sign dictionary from unembeddings nearly matches a Gemma Scope SAE on sparse probing. V. Nalagatla et al., 2026 ↗
Compressed and distilled students do not fully match the teacher 3 studies

Adapting a model can make a fixed feature dictionary describe it more faithfully. A student distilled at equal or smaller capacity need not recover the teacher's units, and its loss can level off above zero.

  • Distilled Pythia-410M students plateau at a nonzero KL divergence from the teacher, even at teacher width. Nilesh Sarkar et al., 2026 ↗

Features across models and domains

These findings are for anyone applying features or dictionaries beyond one layer, one model or text: how features carry over, drift or differ across layers, model updates, model families, languages, modalities and non-text domains.

Interpretable sparse features in vision, biology and other domains 62 studies

Sparse dictionaries trained on vision, biology, physics, recommendation and policy models can recover interpretable features. How selective, fine-grained and faithful those features are depends on the model, layer, dataset and evaluation.

  • In a pathology ViT, an SAE feature tracks plasma cells more selectively than a neuron. Nhat Dinh Minh Le et al., 2024 ↗
  • A probe on DNABERT-2 SAE latents classifies CTCF-bound sequences at accuracy 0.7881. Wei-Min Wu et al., 2025 ↗
  • ESM2-650M SAE features match ELM protein motifs at median AUROC 0.80, without neuron or random-model baselines. Chao Hou et al., 2026 ↗
Dictionaries transfer imperfectly across data, models and updates 29 studies

How well a dictionary covers and transfers depends on its training distribution, domain, modality, context, layer and model updates. Fidelity on source activations need not carry over to shifted activations.

  • Base-model SAEs transfer to longer contexts, with MSE up 12%, and to Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct at most layers. Zheng-Fu He et al., 2024 ↗
  • General-corpus SAEs explain less variance on domain and language data than on FineWeb-Edu. N. Koriagin et al., 2025 ↗
  • Base-model Qwen-Scope SAE explains 0.50 of Instruct residual variance; an earlier 0.82 used the wrong hook. V. Kazei, 2026 ↗
Models share some features, but alignment is partial 26 studies

Different models can share partly alignable semantic structure while differing in individual directions. How much is shared depends on training, architecture, layer and matching method; shared geometry does not guarantee the features work interchangeably.

  • Two SAEs on the same CLIP-ViT-B/32 encoder align far above a shuffled control. Clément Cornet et al., 2025 ↗
  • Features shared across models predict functional sites better than architecture-unique ones (AUROC 0.925 vs 0.661). Jacob L. Steenwyk, 2026 ↗
  • Cross-language SAE feature sharing is 87–96% in Gemma-3-4B but 4–6% in Llama-3.2-3B. Igor Bogdanov et al., 2026 ↗
Features persist, drift and recur across layers 20 studies

Features can persist, shift, merge or reappear across layers. Single-layer reconstructions and decoder norms can miss token-dependent drift between layers, and the same feature repeated at several layers.

  • Multi-layer SAE features spread across layers in aggregate (variance ratio 54–88%) but not per token (1–10%). Tim Lawson et al., 2024 ↗
  • Bishop-move features recur at three chess-model layers; ablating one does little, masking all lowers target-move probability. Rui Lin et al., 2026 ↗
Feature roles change with depth and model scale 17 studies

Dictionary features differ in token alignment, abstraction, role, dynamics and sharing across depth and model scale. Features emerge, split and persist unevenly.

  • In a small LM, deeper SAE features are less concept-selective: top concepts lead runners-up by less. Mariam Mahran et al., 2025 ↗
  • French and German backdoor-trigger features overlap in 13 of 27 layers (8B model), none at 1B. Wissam Antoun et al., 2026 ↗
Features persist or drift as models keep training 15 studies

Dictionary features can persist across model updates, but their activations, geometry and causal roles can drift with continued training, fine-tuning and pruning.

  • Across Pythia training, broad early SAE features persist far more often than narrow ones. P. Stecher et al., 2026 ↗
Multimodal models mix shared and modality-specific features 14 studies

Multimodal representations can contain both shared and modality-specific components. Alignment and transfer depend on token modality, layer, thresholds and post-training, and features that fire together need not point the same way.

  • SAE latents labeled multimodal range from 23 to 223 depending on the threshold. Sergio Lanza et al., 2026 ↗
  • Aligned text-side SAE directions steer LLaVA captions at layer 25; an unaligned SAE at matched sparsity never succeeds. Huizhen Shu et al., 2026 ↗
Features can be shared across languages or language-specific 11 studies

Features can be shared across languages or specific to one. Their activation and causal effects depend on concept, task, depth, linguistic context, resource level and training.

  • Ablating two language-specific SAE directions mainly hurts the target language in Gemma 2 and Llama-3.1. Boyi Deng et al., 2025 ↗
  • In Gemma-2-2B, SAE activations are lower on text translated into lower-resource languages than on high-resource-language text. Richmond Sin Jing Xuan et al., 2025 ↗
Vision embeddings partly compose by vector addition 4 studies

Some vision and text-to-image embeddings support approximate vector composition and separate word senses, while similar concepts and attributes can blend or interfere.

  • Composite-image MedCLIP embeddings are rebuilt from component embeddings at cosine similarity 0.97. Riccardo Renzulli et al., 2025 ↗
Vision activations cluster meaning locally; findings depend on method 4 studies

Semantic structure in vision activations shows up in local regions of activation space, at class boundaries and in scene components shared across channels. What is found also depends on the analysis or reconstruction method.

  • Images reconstructed from deep-layer channels share a large component; subtracting the cross-channel mean mostly removes it. Kai-Xiang Shu, 2026 ↗

Where to start reading

  1. 1

    Nelson Elhage et al., 2022 ↗ Toy Models of Superposition

    The original toy-model study: feature sparsity and importance shape superposition and its geometry. Read phase diagrams with the linear comparison.

  2. 2

    Adam Scherlis et al., 2022 ↗ Polysemanticity and Capacity in Neural Networks

    A second toy model (quadratic), analyzed and simulated, showing when features get their own dimension, share dimensions, or are ignored.

  3. 3

    Victor Lecomte et al., 2023 ↗ What Causes Polysemanticity? An Alternative Origin Story of Mixed Selectivity from Incidental Causes

    Shows in a toy autoencoder that polysemanticity can arise incidentally, without capacity shortage; prevalence in real models is open.

Known gaps in this draft

Main open problems: thin evidence at large scale; unresolved or merely apparent disagreements about feature reproducibility, geometry and interpretability; challenges that are counterexamples rather than failed replications; unread or unverified sources; possible new claims whose independence is unchecked; and misread findings and duplicate records not all fixed.

All 7 gaps
  • Little of the evidence comes from models above 10B parameters, and no study is recorded above 100B. Many studies do not state model size, so conclusions about scale rest on very few studies.
  • Studies disagree on how reproducible SAE features are across training seeds in GPT-2 small: one matches 94% of latents, another finds much lower reproducibility. The two appear to use different dictionary widths, so the gap may reflect width rather than a failed replication.
  • Several challenges to the claims are counterexamples to strong wording, not failed replications. For instance, polysemanticity without a shortage of neurons shows that capacity shortage is not necessary, not that it is never sufficient.
  • Possible disagreements between studies on the same models have not been worked through. Examples are circular weekday features versus a one-dimensional pattern for years in GPT-2 small, which may differ only in the feature studied, and SAEs scoring near chance on word senses versus positive interpretability results.
  • Part of the literature could not be checked: 65 candidate studies could not be retrieved, and parts of the original paper's findings and of Bricken et al.'s sparse-autoencoder study remain unverified. Two relevant studies, one on seed stability by Paulo and Belrose and one arguing that superposition is not necessary, have not yet been assessed against the claims.
  • Some large groups of findings may deserve claims of their own, notably computation in superposition, the link between superposition and adversarial vulnerability, and multidimensional features. Whether these findings come from independent research groups has not been checked.
  • A check of the study findings recorded here found many misreadings, and only those flagged in the summaries were corrected. Duplicate entries for the same study and missed overlaps between author groups also make it unclear how independent the evidence is.
